questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve attached to the lower border of pons above pyramid is:
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) is attached to the lower border of the pons, in the groove between the pons and pyramid of the medulla. It is the most medial of the cranial nerves at the pontomedullary junction.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nerve at lower pons above pyramid

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a recess of the fourth ventricle?
questions.explanation: The lateral recess is the only true recess of the fourth ventricle. It extends laterally beneath the superior cerebellar peduncle and opens at the foramen of Luschka into the subarachnoid space.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral recess is a recess of fourth ventricle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Medial eminence in floor of fourth ventricle overlies the nucleus of:
questions.explanation: The medial eminence overlies the abducent nucleus in the floor of the fourth ventricle. The facial colliculus (a elevation) is formed by the abducent nucleus and the facial nerve fibers looping around it.
questions.keyConcept: Medial eminence overlies abducent nucleus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The superior angle of the fourth ventricle leads to:
questions.explanation: The superior angle of the fourth ventricle is continuous with the cerebral aqueduct (aqueduct of Sylvius), which connects the third and fourth ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Superior 4th ventricle angle leads to cerebral aqueduct

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Brain stem includes all the following Except:
questions.explanation: The brain stem consists of midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata. The cerebellum lies posterior to the brain stem and is not considered part of it, though it is connected by three peduncles.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellum not part of brain stem

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following nerves lies close to the median plane in the transverse furrow between pons and medulla?
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) emerges at the pontomedullary junction, close to the median plane (between the pons and pyramid). It is the most medial of the cranial nerves at this junction.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nerve most medial at pontomedullary junction

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards medulla oblongata, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) lies MEDIAL to the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Rootlets emerge between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle. The statement in option D incorrectly places it lateral to ICP.
questions.keyConcept: Vagus nerve medial to inferior cerebellar peduncle
options: Olive lies just lateral to anterior median fissure.
Inferior cerebellar peduncle lies lateral to olive.
XII cranial nerve exits from medulla lateral to pyramid.
X cranial nerve lies medial to inferior cerebellar peduncle.
XI cranial nerve is attached to posterolateral sulcus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards pons, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: Cerebellopontine angle tumors typically arise from the vestibulocochlear nerve (acoustic neuroma/schwannoma) and cause hearing loss, vertigo, and later facial nerve involvement. Pontine gliomas would cause different symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: CPA tumors cause deafness and vertigo
options: Cerebello-pontine angle gives attachment to VI & VII cranial nerves.
Nervus intermedius is the medial root of the facial nerve.
VIII cranial nerve lies medial to VII cranial nerve.
Its ventral surface shows a sulcus for vertebral artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In dorsal surface of medulla oblongata, choose CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The vestibular trigone lies between the limbs of the inferior fovea in the floor of the fourth ventricle. This is the correct statement about dorsal medullary surface features.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibular trigone between limbs of inferior fovea
options: Gracile tubercle is the most medial structure of open medulla.
Base of open medulla is formed by medullary stria.
Vestibular trigone lies between limbs of inferior fovea.
Hypoglossal trigone forms most medial trigone of superior fovea.
Apex of open medulla is continuous with cerebral aqueduct.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards back of pons, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The medial eminence overlies the abducent nucleus, not the facial nucleus. The facial nucleus lies more laterally and is overlain by the facial colliculus formed by fibers wrapping around the abducent nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Medial eminence overlies abducent nucleus, not facial
options: Its apex is continuous with cerebral acqueduct.
Locus ceruleus lies at upper end of sulcus limitans.
Sulcus limitans lies lateral to medial eminence.
Vestibular area lies lateral to superior fovea.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A collection of ascending fibers in the brain stem form:
questions.explanation: A lemniscus is a collection of sensory fibers that ascend through the brainstem. Examples include the medial lemniscus (fine touch/proprioception), spinal lemniscus (pain/temperature), and trigeminal lemniscus (face sensation).
questions.keyConcept: Lemniscus is collection of ascending fibers in brainstem

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which one of the following is an afferent connection to the inferior colliculus:
questions.explanation: This matching tests midbrain structures: cerebral aqueduct (around which the tectal plate curves); trochlear nucleus (inferior to oculomotor); superior cerebellar peduncle (lateral to red nucleus).
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar peduncle decussates in midbrain

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which one of the following decussations is associated with red nucleus?
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the motor nucleus supplying muscles of the larynx (and pharynx/soft palate). It is the common motor nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI for these muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus supplies laryngeal muscles
options: Decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards the internal structure of the midbrain, choose the CORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. It supplies stylopharyngeus (IX), pharynx/larynx muscles (X), and sternocleidomastoid/trapezius (XI).
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus - common motor for IX, X, XI
options: Parieto-pontine fibers - medial 1/5 of crus cerebri.
Ventral tegmental Decussation - tegmentum at level of inferior colliculus.
Cortico-spinal tract - lateral 1/5 of crus cerebri.
Cortico-nuclear tract - middle 3/5 of crus cerebri.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Tegmentum pontis contains all the following structures EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic nucleus of the glossopharyngeal nerve is the inferior salivary nucleus. It provides parasympathetic innervation to the parotid gland via the otic ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior salivary nucleus - parasympathetic to parotid

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: For each structure in left column, choose its appropriate place in midbrain from right column:
questions.explanation: The somatic efferent column includes: oculomotor nucleus (III), trochlear nucleus (IV), abducent nucleus (VI), and hypoglossal nucleus (XII). These nuclei supply muscles derived from somites.
questions.keyConcept: CN III, IV, VI, XII are somatic efferent nuclei

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Gracile and cuneate nuclei are supplied by medullary branches of:
questions.explanation: The gracile and cuneate nuclei (dorsal column nuclei) are supplied by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) and direct medullary branches of the vertebral artery, not the anterior spinal artery.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinal/PICA supply dorsal column nuclei

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Lateral medullary syndrome includes the following Except:
questions.explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome includes vestibular symptoms (vertigo, nystagmus) due to involvement of the vestibular nuclei. This is a key feature that distinguishes Wallenberg syndrome from medial medullary syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral medullary includes vestibular symptoms
options: Ipsilateral paralysis of palate, pharynx & larynx.
Contralateral pain & temperature loss from face.
Ipsilateral loss of taste of posterior 1/3 of tongue.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The medial medullary syndrome includes:
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome includes: ipsilateral tongue paralysis (hypoglossal), contralateral hemiparesis (pyramidal), and contralateral loss of proprioception/fine touch (medial lemniscus). Pain and temperature are preserved.
questions.keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome includes tongue paralysis
options: Ipsilateral lower motor neuron lesion of XII.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding the medulla oblongata, the medial zone containing the pyramid is supplied by:
questions.explanation: The medial zone of the medulla (containing the pyramid) is supplied by the anterior spinal artery, which runs in the anterior median fissure. The lateral and posterior regions are supplied by vertebral artery branches and PICA.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal supplies medial medulla/pyramid

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe dorsal surface of medulla oblongata.
questions.explanation: The dorsal surface of the medulla oblongata shows: (1) INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - connects medulla to cerebellum; (2) MIDDLE CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - visible at the pontomedullary junction; (3) FLOOR OF FOURTH VENTRICLE: divided into MEDULLARY TRIGONE (containing hypoglossal trigone over hypoglossal nucleus and vagal trigone over dorsal motor nucleus of X) and PONTINE TRIGONE. The gracile and cuneate tubercles (over dorsal column nuclei) are visible above the trigone.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal medulla: inferior/middle cerebellar peduncles, hypoglossal and vagal trigones in fourth ventricle floor
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI IN MEDULLA: (SOMATIC EFFERENT) Hypoglossal nucleus; (VISCERAL EFFERENT) Dorsal motor nucleus of X, inferior salivary nucleus; (VISCERAL AFFERENT) Nucleus solitarius; (TRIGEMINAL) Spinal nucleus of V; (AUDITORY) Cochlear nuclei; (VESTIBULAR) Vestibular nuclei; (OTHER) Olivary nuclei, cuneate/gracile nuclei, accessory cuneate nucleus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe dorsal surface of pons.
questions.explanation: The dorsal surface of the pons forms the upper part of the floor of the fourth ventricle: (1) FACIAL COLLICULUS - elevation over abducens nucleus and facial nerve fibers internally; (2) TRIGEMINAL TUBERCLE - over the principal sensory nucleus of CN V; (3) MEDIAL EMINENCE - longitudinal elevation; (4) SUPERIOR and INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLES form the lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle at this level.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal pons: facial colliculus, trigeminal tubercle, forms upper fourth ventricle floor with peduncles as lateral borders
questions.modelAnswer: INFERIOR OLIVARY COMPLEX: (COMPONENTS) Main olivary nucleus (folded gray matter), medial accessory olivary nucleus, dorsal accessory olivary nucleus; (CONNECTIONS) Receives input from red nucleus, spinal cord, and cerebral cortex; (OUTPUT) Olivocerebellar fibers cross and enter cerebellum via inferior cerebellar peduncle; (FUNCTION) Involved in motor learning and coordination.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe dorsal surface of midbrain.
questions.explanation: The dorsal surface of the midbrain (tectum) shows the quadrigeminal plate (corpora quadrigemina): (1) SUPERIOR COLLICULI - visual reflexes (paired); (2) INFERIOR COLLICULI - auditory pathway. Below the inferior colliculi are the superior cerebellar peduncles. The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally, emerging between the two inferior colliculi.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal midbrain: quadrigeminal plate (superior and inferior colliculi); CN IV exits dorsally
questions.modelAnswer: STRUCTURES IN BASIS PONTIS: (1) Longitudinal fibers - corticopontine, corticospinal, corticobulbar; (2) Transverse fibers - pontocerebellar fibers linking pons with cerebellum; (3) Pontine nuclei - gray matter between fiber bundles; (4) Basilar artery runs in basilar sulcus; (5) CN V attaches at lateral surface.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate internal features of medulla oblongata.
questions.explanation: Internal features of the medulla oblongata include: (1) PYRAMIDS - containing corticospinal fibers, located on either side of anterior median fissure; (2) OLVES - containing inferior olivary nuclei; (3) INTERNAL ARCUATE FIBERS - decussating sensory fibers from dorsal column nuclei; (4) MEDIAL LEMNISCUS - formed after sensory decussation, ascends through brainstem; (5) CRANIAL NERVE NUCLEI: hypoglossal, dorsal motor nucleus of X, nucleus solitarius, nucleus ambiguus, inferior salivary nucleus; (6) INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLES laterally.
questions.keyConcept: Medulla internal features: pyramids, olives, internal arcuate fibers, medial lemniscus, cranial nerve nuclei
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL NERVE: (1) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (SVE) - motor to stylopharyngeus muscle; (2) INFERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic to parotid gland via otic ganglion; (3) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (SVA/GVA) - taste from posterior 1/3 of tongue and visceral sensation; (4) SPINAL NUCLEUS OF V (GSA) - general sensation from middle ear, pharynx.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe pyramidal decussation.
questions.explanation: Pyramidal decussation: LOCATION at the caudal medulla where the medulla transitions to the spinal cord. PROCESS: About 85-90% of corticospinal fibers cross obliquely in the anterior median fissure. RESULT: Crossed fibers form the lateral corticospinal tract in the lateral white column; uncrossed fibers remain as the anterior corticospinal tract. CLINICAL: This decussation explains why unilateral cerebral lesions cause contralateral motor deficits.
questions.keyConcept: Pyramidal decussation: 85-90% of corticospinal fibers cross at caudal medulla to form lateral CST
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF FACIAL NERVE: (1) FACIAL MOTOR NUCLEUS (SVE) - motor to muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric; (2) SUPERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic to lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands; (3) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (SVA) - taste from anterior 2/3 of tongue; (4) MESENCEPHALIC NUCLEUS OF V - proprioception from facial muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate nuclei in medulla oblongata.
questions.explanation: Nuclei in the medulla oblongata include: (1) HYPOGLOSSAL NUCLEUS (somatic efferent) - in floor near central canal, supplies tongue muscles; (2) DORSAL MOTOR NUCLEUS OF X (visceral efferent) - parasympathetic to thoracic/abdominal viscera; (3) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (special visceral efferent) - motor to pharynx/larynx; (4) INFERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (visceral efferent) - parasympathetic to parotid; (5) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (visceral afferent) - taste and general visceral sensation; (6) SPINAL NUCLEUS OF V (general somatic afferent); (7) COCHLEAR and VESTIBULAR NUCLEI; (8) GRACILE and CUNEATE NUCLEI; (9) ACCESSORY CUNEATE NUCLEUS.
questions.keyConcept: Medullary nuclei: hypoglossal, dorsal motor X, nucleus ambiguus, inferior salivary, nucleus solitarius, cochlear/vestibular nuclei
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF OCULOMOTOR NERVE: (1) OCULOMOTOR NUCLEUS (SSE) - motor to superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique muscles; (2) EDINGER-WESTPHAL NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic to sphincter pupillae (pupil constriction) and ciliary muscle (accommodation); (3) Central caudal nucleus - coordinates function.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate structures in tegmentum pontis.
questions.explanation: Structures in the tegmentum pontis include: (1) CRANIAL NERVE NUCLEI: Abducens nucleus (CN VI), Facial nucleus (CN VII), Vestibular nuclei (CN VIII), Cochlear nuclei (CN VIII); (2) TRACT: Medial longitudinal fasciculus; (3) LEMNISCI: Medial lemniscus, trigeminal lemniscus; (4) NUCLEI: Superior olivary nucleus (sound localization), nuclei of reticular formation; (5) TRAPEZOID BODY (auditory pathway); (6) The pyramid does NOT continue here (interrupted by transverse pontocerebellar fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Tegmentum pontis: CN VI, VII, VIII nuclei, medial lemniscus, superior olivary nucleus, reticular formation
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF GVE COLUMN: (1) EDINGER-WESTPHAL NUCLEUS (III) - ciliary and pterygopalatine ganglia (eye, lacrimal); (2) SUPERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (VII) - submandibular and sublingual glands; (3) INFERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (IX) - otic ganglion to parotid; (4) DORSAL MOTOR NUCLEUS OF X - thoracic and abdominal viscera.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe parts of midbrain & enumerate structures within each part.
questions.explanation: The midbrain has three parts: (1) TECTUM (quadrigeminal plate) - dorsal, contains superior colliculus (visual reflexes) and inferior colliculus (auditory relay); (2) TEGMENTUM - between tectum and crus cerebri, contains crus cerebri, substantia nigra, red nucleus, RAPPORT decussation, medial lemniscus, and decussations of superior cerebellar peduncle and red nucleus; (3) CRUS CEREBRI (cerebral peduncle) - ventral, contains descending motor fibers (frontopontine most medial, corticospinal/corticobulbar middle, parieto/temporopontine most lateral).
questions.keyConcept: Midbrain parts: tectum (colliculi), tegmentum (red nucleus, substantia nigra), crus cerebri (descending fibers)
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF GSA COLUMN: (1) TRIGEMINAL NUCLEI (principal and spinal) - face, head; (2) COCHLEAR NUCLEI - hearing; (3) VESTIBULAR NUCLEI - balance; (4) SPINAL NUCLEUS OF V - general sensation from head and face. All receive general somatic afferent fibers from head and neck region.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate tegmental decussations of midbrain.
questions.explanation: Tegmental decussations of the midbrain include: (1) DECUSSATION OF SUPERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - dentate nucleus output to thalamus crosses in midbrain; (2) DECUSSATION OF RED NUCLEUS (rubrobulbar and rubospinal tracts) - crosses just below superior colliculus; (3) TROCHLEAR NERVE DECUSSATION - CN IV is unique as the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally and completely cross before emerging. These decussations are part of the extrapyramidal motor system.
questions.keyConcept: Tegmental decussations: superior cerebellar peduncle, red nucleus, and trochlear nerve (only dorsal-exiting CN)
questions.modelAnswer: MEDIAL MEDULLARY SYNDROME: (CAUSE) Occlusion of anterior spinal artery or vertebral artery; (SIGNS) IPSILATERAL: tongue paralysis (hypoglossal nerve); CONTRALATERAL: UMN paralysis of body (pyramidal tract), loss of proprioception and fine touch (medial lemniscus); (PRESERVED) Pain and temperature (spinothalamic intact), dorsal column for upper levels.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe the arterial supply of medulla oblongata.
questions.explanation: The foramen ovale gives passage to emissary veins connecting the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid plexus of veins. This provides a route for infection spread from face to meninges.
questions.keyConcept: Foramen ovale has emissary veins of cavernous sinus
questions.modelAnswer: ARTERIAL SUPPLY OF MEDULLA: (1) ANTERIOR SPINAL ARTERY → supplies medial medulla (pyramids, medial lemniscus, hypoglossal nucleus) - thrombosis causes medial medullary syndrome; (2) VERTEBRAL ARTERIES → supply lateral surfaces; (3) POSTERIOR INFERIOR CEREBELLAR ARTERY (PICA) → supplies lateral medulla (olive, inferior cerebellar peduncle, vestibular/cochlear nuclei) - thrombosis causes lateral medullary syndrome; (4) Direct medullary branches from vertebral arteries.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Give a brief note on medial medullary syndrome.
questions.explanation: Infection from mastoid air cells typically spreads to the sigmoid sinus (which runs in the groove for the sigmoid sinus in the mastoid). This can cause sinus thrombosis and meningitis.
questions.keyConcept: Mastoid infection spreads to sigmoid sinus
questions.modelAnswer: MEDIAL MEDULLARY SYNDROME: (CAUSE) Anterior spinal artery or bilateral vertebral artery occlusion; (SIGNS): IPSILATERAL: complete paralysis and atrophy of tongue (CN XII); CONTRALATERAL: spastic paralysis of body (pyramidal tract), loss of proprioception and discriminative touch (medial lemniscus); (PRESERVED): pain, temperature, and crude touch (spinothalamic tracts intact bilaterally).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The fourth ventricle is connected to the third ventricle by:
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius is the narrow channel that passes through the midbrain and connects the third ventricle anteriorly with the fourth ventricle posteriorly. It is flanked by the cerebral peduncles and is the most common site of obstruction in non-communicating hydrocephalus.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct connects 3rd ventricle (anterior) with 4th ventricle (posterior).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient comes to the emergency room with a laceration on the scalp following a head injury. The wound appears to be bleeding profusely. Which layer of the scalp is primarily responsible for this bleeding?
questions.explanation: The subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia) of the scalp is highly vascular because it contains the arteries and veins of the scalp embedded in a firm fatty layer. This layer has rich anastomoses between the supraorbital, superficial temporal, and occipital arteries. The skin containsplexuses but the profuse bleeding in scalp lacerations is mainly from this highly vascular subcutaneous layer. The galea'subgaleal layer is avascular and the pericranium is thin.
questions.keyConcept: Subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia) of scalp is highly vascular; main source of profuse bleeding in scalp injuries due to arterial anastomoses.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with a complaint of persistent numbness and tingling on the posterior aspect of their scalp, especially on the left side behind the ear. They report no other neurological symptoms. Which nerve is likely responsible for this sensation?
questions.explanation: The lesser occipital nerve is a branch of the cervical plexus (C2) that supplies the skin of the scalp posterior to the ear and the upper part of the lateral surface of the auricle. The greater occipital nerve (C2) supplies the posterior scalp near the midline. The posterior auricular nerve (branch of CN VII) supplies behind the ear.
questions.keyConcept: Lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the scalp posterior and lateral to the ear (posterolateral scalp).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which part of the spinal cord is responsible for transmitting motor signals to the muscles that control fine movements of the fingers and hands?
questions.explanation: Fine movements of the fingers and hands are controlled by the C8-T1 spinal cord segments, which give rise to the ulnar and median nerves. The cervical region of the spinal cord (C5-T1) is enlarged at the cervicothoracic junction (intumescence) specifically to accommodate the large number of motor neurons for the upper limbs. The lumbar region controls the lower limbs.
questions.keyConcept: Finger/hand fine movements = CERVICAL spinal cord region (especially C8-T1); cervical enlargement supplies upper limb nerves.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 44-year-old female patient has a lesion in the right cerebral peduncle in the midbrain. She would present with a loss of:
questions.explanation: The corticospinal tract decussates at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla. After decussation, the fibers descend in the lateral column of the spinal cord. A right cerebral peduncle lesion affects fibers that have NOT yet decussated, therefore causing CONTRALATERAL (left-sided) motor weakness. The corticospinal fibers to the lower limb are most medial in the peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral peduncle contains corticospinal fibers BEFORE their decussation in the medulla; right peduncle lesion = LEFT-sided weakness.

fine touch and pain sensation from the entire right side of the body

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The neurotransmitter used by the axons of substantia nigra neurons which project to the caudate and putamen is :
questions.explanation: The neurotransmitter used by substantia nigra neurons projecting to caudate and putamen is dopamine. Option C is correct. These neurons form the nigrostriatal pathway. When they degenerate (as in Parkinson's), dopamine levels in the striatum drop, causing motor symptoms. Option A is wrong (ACh is used locally in striatum). Options B, D, E are wrong neurotransmitters for this pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine is the nigrostriatal neurotransmitter; its deficiency causes Parkinson's disease motor symptoms.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the best choice for patients with dementia due to substantia nigra lesion (Parkinson’s disease)?
questions.explanation: Rivastigmine is a centrally acting cholinesterase inhibitor FDA‑approved for dementia associated with Parkinson's disease, targeting the cholinergic deficit caused by basal forebrain degeneration.
questions.keyConcept: Rivastigmine is the cholinesterase inhibitor of choice for Parkinson's disease dementia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which ion is primarily responsible for rapid depolarization during an action potential?
questions.explanation: Sodium (Na+) influx through voltage-gated channels drives the rapid upstroke of the neuronal action potential. When threshold is reached, Nav1.5/1.2 channels open, causing rapid depolarization from -70 mV toward +30 mV.
questions.keyConcept: Sodium ion influx through voltage-gated Na+ channels is responsible for the rapid depolarization phase of the action potential.

questions.explanation: The inverse stretch reflex (Golgi tendon reflex) is a protective mechanism that prevents muscle damage from excessive contraction. It involves Golgi tendon organs (GTOs) detecting tension, Ib afferent fibers, and interneurons that inhibit alpha motor neurons (disynaptic). Unlike the stretch reflex which responds to stretch, the inverse stretch reflex responds to tension. When tension becomes dangerous, it causes reflex relaxation of the contracting muscle. The stretch reflex maintains tone and resists stretching, while the inverse stretch reflex prevents contractile damage. Clinical application: In clasp-knife reflex (upper motor neuron lesion), initially there's resistance (stretch reflex activation), then sudden release (inverse stretch reflex overpowers due to excessive tension).
questions.keyConcept: The inverse stretch reflex (Golgi tendon reflex) protects muscles from excessive contraction by causing reflex relaxation via Ib afferents.

Types: 1) Non-associative learning: habituation (decreased response to repeated stimulus) and sensitization (increased response after strong or novel stimulus). Mechanism: habituation involves decreased neurotransmitter release at sensory neuron synapses; sensitization involves facilitation of synaptic transmission; 2) Associative learning: classical conditioning (Pavlovian - pairing neutral with unconditioned stimulus) and operant/instrumental conditioning (behavior reinforced by rewards/punishments). Mechanism of classical conditioning: associative plasticity in cerebellum (deep nuclei and Purkinje cells) and amygdala for emotional conditioning. questions.keyConcept: Learning includes non-associative (habituation, sensitization) and associative (classical, operant) types, mediated by synaptic plasticity.

Has a sleep center in its upper part.
Non-specifically activates the whole cortex, mainly directly.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Medullary reticular formation is stimulated by:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding the fourth ventricle
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle is the cavity of the hindbrain (rhombencephalon), communicates with third ventricle above and subarachnoid space below via median/lateral apertures, and has a roof and floor.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle features
options: Is the cavity of hind brain

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The processes of protoplasmic astrocytes are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Protoplasmic astrocytes (found in grey matter) have numerous short, branching processes. Fibrous astrocytes (found in white matter) have few long, thin processes.
questions.keyConcept: Protoplasmic astrocytes: numerous short branching processes (grey matter)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Tanycytes line which of the following:
questions.explanation: Tanycytes are specialized ependymal cells that line the floor of the third ventricle, particularly in the infundibular recess. They have long basal processes and are thought to transport substances between the ventricle and hypothalamic nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Tanycytes line the third ventricle floor, involved in neuroendocrine transport

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The apical surface of ependymal cells has:
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells have cilia on their apical surfaces that help circulate cerebrospinal fluid. The coordinated beating of these cilia moves CSF through the ventricular system.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal cells have cilia on apical surface for CSF circulation

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The basal surface of tanycytes has:
questions.explanation: Tanycytes have long basal processes that extend to blood vessels and hypothalamic nuclei, allowing them to transport substances between the CSF and blood/hypothalamus. This makes them specialized for neuroendocrine communication.
questions.keyConcept: Tanycytes have basal processes for transport between ventricle and hypothalamus

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: All of the followings have choroid plexus EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct connects the third and fourth ventricles but does not have choroid plexus (it is too narrow). Choroid plexus is present in the lateral ventricles, third ventricle, and fourth ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct lacks choroid plexus (no choroid plexus EXCEPT in aqueduct)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The central canal is lined by:
questions.explanation: The central canal is lined by simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium that is partially ciliated (ependymal cells). This is the remnant of the embryonic neural tube lumen.
questions.keyConcept: Central canal lined by simple columnar to cuboidal partially ciliated epithelium
options: Simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium partially ciliated.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The oligodendrocyte is derived from ... while microglia is derived from ...
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm, while microglia are derived from mesoderm (monocyte-macrophage lineage). This distinction is clinically relevant for CNS pathology.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes from ectoderm, microglia from mesoderm

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following cells produce myelin sheath?
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes form myelin sheaths in the CNS (one oligodendrocyte myelinates multiple axons). Schwann cells produce myelin in the PNS. Astrocytes provide structural support; ependymal cells line ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes produce myelin in CNS (Schwann cells in PNS)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: In the CNS, which of the following are phagocytic cells?
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident phagocytic cells of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in CNS injury and disease, acting as macrophages. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes are not phagocytic.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia are the phagocytic cells of CNS (mesodermal origin)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: In the CNS injury, which of the following cells are abundant?
questions.explanation: After CNS injury, astrocytes (forming glial scars) and activated microglia (phagocytic response) increase in number. This reactive gliosis is a hallmark of CNS injury response.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes and microglia are abundant in CNS injury (reactive gliosis)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Endothelial cells of blood capillaries in brain characterized by having:
questions.explanation: Brain capillary endothelial cells have few pinocytic vesicles, abundant mitochondria, tight junctions (forming the blood-brain barrier), and few desmosomes. The tight junctions prevent paracellular diffusion.
questions.keyConcept: Brain endothelium has tight junctions (blood-brain barrier) not few tight junctions

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is involved in the blood-brain barrier?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes are involved in the blood-brain barrier, through their end-feet which induce and maintain tight junctions between endothelial cells. Ependymal cells form the blood-CSF barrier, not the blood-brain barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes are involved in blood-brain barrier structure and function

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The distribution of grey and white matter depends on the distribution of:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers; white matter contains myelinated fibers. The distribution of myelin (lipid-rich insulating material) determines the distinction between grey and white matter.
questions.keyConcept: Myelin distribution determines grey vs white matter distribution

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the following is a component of Blood CSF barrier:
questions.explanation: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by tight junctions between ependymal cells. The arachnoid membrane and its cells lack tight junctions and do not form a barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form blood-CSF barrier

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the followings is not present in grey matter:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cells, neuroglial cells, and unmyelinated nerve fibers. Myelinated nerve fibers are characteristic of white matter, not grey matter.
questions.keyConcept: Myelinated nerve fibers NOT present in grey matter (white matter characteristic)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Inner pyramidal cells are present in layer .... of cerebral cortex:
questions.explanation: Inner pyramidal cells (also called giant pyramidal cells or Betz cells in motor cortex) are found in layer V of the cerebral cortex. They give rise to corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Inner pyramidal cells in layer V of cerebral cortex (corticospinal origin)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Cranial nerve nucleus in floor of 4th ventricle close to midline in lower pons is:
questions.explanation: The abducent nucleus (CN VI) is located in the floor of the fourth ventricle close to the midline in the lower pons. It supplies the lateral rectus muscle of the eye.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nucleus in floor of 4th ventricle, close to midline, lower pons

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The first order neurons for pain and temperature pathway from face and head are located in:
questions.explanation: The first-order neurons for pain and temperature from the face are located in the trigeminal ganglion (Gasserian ganglion). Their central processes enter the pons and synapse in the spinal nucleus of trigeminal.
questions.keyConcept: First-order pain/temperature neurons for face in trigeminal ganglion

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The most of V nerve nuclei are best seen in:
questions.explanation: The main sensory and spinal nuclei of the trigeminal nerve are best seen in the upper pons at the level of the entry of the trigeminal nerve. The mesencephalic nucleus extends into the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal nerve nuclei best seen in upper pons (entry zone)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The only cranial nerve that decussates before its emergence is:
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that decussates (crosses) in the brainstem before emerging from the dorsal surface of the midbrain. This is unique among cranial nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that decussates before emergence

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The first order neurons in proprioception pathway from face and head are in:
questions.explanation: The first-order neurons for proprioception from the face and head are located in the mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve. This is unique as these are the only sensory neuron cell bodies located within the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus (trigeminal) contains 1st order proprioception neurons for face

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Internal arcuate fibers are present in:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are present in the medulla (open medulla), where they arise from the gracile and cuneate nuclei, decussate (cross the midline), and ascend as the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers present in medulla (decussate to form medial lemniscus)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Each of the following statements concerning closed medulla is true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: In the closed medulla, the main inferior olivary nucleus is present, and it contains the gracile and cuneate nuclei on the dorsal aspect. The motor decussation is in the lower part, and sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibers) is at a higher level - making 'higher level has sensory decussation' TRUE, not the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Closed medulla: motor decussation lower, sensory decussation at higher level
options: In the lower part, there are motor decussation.
At a higher level, there are sensory decussation.
Contains the main inferior olivary nucleus.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Cranial nerves in medulla oblongata are the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Cranial nerves with nuclei in the medulla are IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory), and XII (hypoglossal). The facial nerve (VII) has its nuclei in the pons, not the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve (VII) has nuclei in pons, NOT medulla - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Gracile & Cuneate N. are present in:
questions.explanation: The gracile and cuneate nuclei are present on the dorsal aspect of the closed medulla, where they receive input from the fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus respectively. These nuclei are relay stations in the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile and cuneate nuclei on dorsal aspect of closed medulla

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Crossing fibers of gracile & cuneate tracts are called:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are the decussating fibers from the gracile and cuneate nuclei that cross in the medulla to form the medial lemniscus. External arcuate fibers are different (pontocerebellar and olivocerebellar fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers are crossing fibers from gracile and cuneate nuclei

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Lowermost level of medulla shows:
questions.explanation: The lowermost level of the medulla (pyramidal decussation level) shows decussating corticospinal fibers crossing from one pyramid to the other. Internal arcuate fibers are seen at higher levels; inferior olive is above this level.
questions.keyConcept: Lowermost medulla shows corticospinal fiber decussation (pyramidal decussation)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Arcuate nucleus is found in:
questions.explanation: The arcuate nucleus is found ventral to the pyramids in the medulla. It is a small nucleus that gives rise to some of the ventral external arcuate fibers that enter the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Arcuate nucleus found ventral to pyramids in medulla

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from:
questions.explanation: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from the accessory cuneate nucleus (lateral cuneate nucleus), which receives input from the upper limb. They enter the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from accessory cuneate nucleus

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The central gray in upper closed medulla contains:
questions.explanation: The central gray in the upper closed medulla contains the inferior olivary nucleus, which is a major source of climbing fibers to the cerebellum. The spinal nucleus of V is more lateral; nucleus solitarius is more caudal.
questions.keyConcept: Central gray in upper closed medulla contains inferior olivary nucleus

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Internal arcuate fibers are seen in:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers (decussating sensory fibers from gracile and cuneate nuclei) are seen in the lower level of closed medulla. At this level, they cross to form the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers seen in lower closed medulla (sensory decussation)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The reticular formation controls the endocrine system due to its connections with:
questions.explanation: The reticular formation influences the endocrine system through its extensive connections with the hypothalamus. This hypothalamic-reticular connection controls autonomic functions and hormone release.
questions.keyConcept: Reticular formation connects to hypothalamus to control endocrine system

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the relays nuclei of auditory pathway is:
questions.explanation: The superior olivary nucleus is a relay nucleus in the auditory pathway, located in the pons. It receives input from the cochlear nuclei and projects to the inferior colliculus via the lateral lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Superior olivary nucleus is a relay in auditory pathway (pons)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Sections in lower level of pons show:
questions.explanation: Sections at the lower level of pons show the middle cerebellar peduncle (entering), vestibular nuclei (medial and inferior), and facial nerve nucleus. The superior cerebellar peduncle is at higher midbrain levels.
questions.keyConcept: Lower pons: middle cerebellar peduncle, medial and inferior vestibular nuclei

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Basis pontis contain the following except:
questions.explanation: Basis pontis contains longitudinal fibers (corticospinal, corticonuclear, reticulospinal) and pontine nuclei. Transverse pontine fibers are pontocerebellar fibers that arise from pontine nuclei and cross to enter the middle cerebellar peduncle - they are NOT in basis pontis.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse pontine fibers NOT in basis pontis (they arise from pontine nuclei)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Auditory pathways contain the following except:
questions.explanation: Auditory pathways include: cochlear nuclei, superior olivary nucleus, lateral lemniscus, and inferior colliculus. The medial lemniscus is somatosensory (touch, proprioception), not auditory.
questions.keyConcept: Medial lemniscus is somatosensory, NOT part of auditory pathway - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: About substantia nigra, all true except:
questions.explanation: The substantia nigra is present in the midbrain, ventral to the cerebral peduncle (not dorsal to basis pontis). It consists of pars compacta (dark, melanin-containing) and pars reticularis. It is connected to the basal ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: Substantia nigra ventral to cerebral peduncle, NOT dorsal to basis pontis - FALSE

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The superior colliculus of midbrain is formed of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The superior colliculus has layers: stratum zonale (superficial), stratum opticum, stratum lemnisci, and stratum basale (deep). The dorsal tegmental tract is a fiber tract, not part of the colliculus structure.
questions.keyConcept: Superior colliculus layers: zonale, opticum, lemnisci, basale (NOT dorsal tegmental tract)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The tract in MLB responsible for head righting reflex is:
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract (from superior colliculus) crosses at the midbrain and descends to cervical spinal cord, mediating head-righting reflexes in response to visual stimuli. This is the tract responsible for head righting reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract in ML mediates head righting reflex

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The specific feature of upper midbrain is presence of:
questions.explanation: The upper midbrain (superior colliculus level) has the crus cerebri (cerebral peduncle) on its ventral aspect, containing corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers. Substantia nigra and red nucleus are at this level but not specific to upper midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Upper midbrain specific feature: crus cerebri (cerebral peduncle)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Central tegmental tract contains fibers connecting between:
questions.explanation: The central tegmental tract contains fibers connecting the red nucleus to the inferior olivary nucleus. It is involved in the dentato-rubro-olivary circuit that modulates cerebellar function.
questions.keyConcept: Central tegmental tract connects red nucleus to inferior olivary nucleus

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Superior cerebellar decussation:
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar decussation (decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles) is present at the inferior level of the midbrain. Tectospinal tract decussates at the midbrain but is not the superior cerebellar decussation.
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar decussation at inferior midbrain level (superior cerebellar peduncles)
options: Present in inferior level of midbrain.
Its fibers descend in all segments of spinal cord.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Superior colliculus, all true except:
questions.explanation: The superior colliculus gives rise to the tectospinal tract and the dorsal tegmental tract. It is composed of small and large neurons, connected with the retina (via optic tract) and occipital cortex (via corticotectal fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Superior colliculus gives tectospinal and dorsal tegmental tracts (NOT an exception)
options: Give tectospinal tract & dorsal tegmental tract.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Inferior olivary nucleus:
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary nucleus receives rubro-olivary fibers through the central tegmental tract. Its efferent fibers (climbing fibers) reach the contralateral cerebellar cortex through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior olivary nucleus receives from red nucleus via central tegmental tract
options: Receive rubro-olivary fibers through the central tegmental tract.
Present in the ventral aspect of closed medulla.
Its efferent fibers reach the ipsilateral cerebellar cortex through the superior cerebellar peduncle.
Its efferent fibers are the mossy fibers reaching the cerebellar cortex.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Medial longitudinal bundle, all true except:
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) extends from the brainstem to the upper cervical segments (not the entire spinal cord). It connects vestibular nuclei to the spinal cord for head and neck movement coordination.
questions.keyConcept: MLF extends to cervical spinal cord, NOT the whole length of spinal cord - FALSE
options: Receive ascending & descending fibers from vestibular nuclei.
Function for movement of the head & neck.
Extending from brainstem till cervical segments of spinal cord.
Extend the whole length of spinal cord.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Dorsal tegmental decussation:
questions.explanation: The dorsal tegmental decussation is formed by the tectospinal tract at the inferior midbrain level. The rubrospinal tract decussates more ventrally (ventral tegmental decussation).
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal tegmental decussation formed by tectospinal tract at inferior midbrain
options: Its fibers descend in all segments of spinal cord.
Present in inferior level of midbrain.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is a WHO grade IV tumor?
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is a WHO grade IV tumor (most malignant), occurring in the cerebellum, especially in children. It is a small round blue cell tumor with high mitotic activity and can metastasize via CSF.
questions.keyConcept: Medulloblastoma is WHO grade IV malignant cerebellar tumor

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which ion is primarily responsible for rapid depolarization during an action potential?
questions.explanation: Sodium ions (Na+) rapidly influx through voltage-gated sodium channels during phase 0 of the action potential, causing depolarization. Potassium efflux causes repolarization (phase 3). Calcium channels contribute to plateau phase in cardiac muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Voltage-gated sodium channels mediate the rapid depolarization phase of action potentials in most neurons and muscle fibers.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The reticular formation is responsible for:
questions.explanation: The reticular formation in the brainstem regulates arousal, sleep-wake cycles, and consciousness through ascending reticular activating system projections to the thalamus and cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Reticular formation maintains consciousness and sleep-arousal cycles via diffuse subcortical projections.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is primarily responsible for rapid depolarization during an action potential?
questions.explanation: Sodium ions (Na+) rapidly influx through voltage-gated sodium channels during phase 0 of the action potential, causing depolarization. Potassium efflux causes repolarization (phase 3). Calcium channels contribute to plateau phase in cardiac muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Voltage-gated sodium channels mediate the rapid depolarization phase of action potentials in most neurons and muscle fibers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Proprioceptive sensation from the big toe ascends to the brainstem through which fibers?
questions.explanation: Proprioception from the lower limb ascends via the gracile fasciculus in the posterior columns to the gracile nucleus in the medulla, then decussates as internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile fasciculus carries lower limb proprioception to the medulla before decussation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which structure is responsible for fine skilled movements of the index finger?
questions.explanation: The corticospinal tract originates from motor cortex including the precentral gyrus and premotor areas. The hand representation in area 4 controls skilled finger movements through lateral corticospinal fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Skilled hand movements are mediated by corticospinal neurons in the precentral gyrus hand area.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Head rotation in response to visual stimuli, with crossing at the level of the superior colliculus, is mediated by which tract?
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract decussates at the superior medullary velum (rostral medulla), which is at the level of the midbrain-pons junction, not the midbrain itself.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract decussates at the level of the inferior colliculus/superior medullary velum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Decussation at the level of the superior midbrain occurs in which of the following tracts?
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique in that it exits the midbrain dorsally and decussates completely before emerging. The oculomotor nerve exits ventrally. Other cranial nerves exit at pontine or medullary levels.
questions.keyConcept: CN IV is the only cranial nerve that decussates and exits dorsally from the midbrain.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery and its branches are primarily responsible for supplying the pons?
questions.explanation: The basilar artery and its branches (paramedian and circumferential pontine arteries) supply the pons. The anterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the anteroinferior pons, while superior cerebellar artery supplies the upper pons.
questions.keyConcept: Basilar artery supplies pons through paramedian and circumferential branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is present in the dorsal surface of the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The corpora quadrigemina (superior and inferior colliculi) are on the dorsal midbrain surface. The basis pedunculi (cerebral peduncles) are on the ventral surface.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal midbrain features include the four colliculi (corpora quadrigemina) for visual and auditory reflexes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which part of the fourth ventricle contains the choroid plexus?
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus in the fourth ventricle is located in the roof (posterior/inferior border), specifically along the tela choroidea and in the lateral recesses near the foramina of Luschka.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle choroid plexus is found in the tela choroidea of the ventricular roof.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures connects the fourth ventricle to the subarachnoid space?
questions.explanation: The foramen of Magendie is the median aperture connecting the fourth ventricle to the subarachnoid space (cisterna magna), allowing CSF flow from the ventricle to the basal cisterns.
questions.keyConcept: Median aperture (Magendie) connects fourth ventricle to subarachnoid space at the cisterna magna.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures forms the roof of the fourth ventricle?
questions.explanation: The roof of the fourth ventricle consists of the superior cerebellar peduncles laterally and the tela choroidea with choroid plexus inferiorly. The floor is formed by the pons and upper medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof comprises cerebellar peduncles and tela choroidea with choroid plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following nuclei, located in the midbrain, contains general visceral efferent (GVE) fibers?
questions.explanation: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus (accessory oculomotor nucleus) is located in the midbrain and contains preganglionic parasympathetic neurons that supply the ciliary and sphincter pupillae muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Edinger-Westphal nucleus provides parasympathetic innervation to intraocular muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arteries supplies the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The midbrain is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and its branches, including the posterior communicating artery. The basilar artery supplies the upper midbrain through its superior cerebellar artery branch.
questions.keyConcept: PCA and basilar artery branches supply the midbrain via posterior circulation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: CSF produced in the fourth ventricle flows into which subarachnoid space via its three foramina?
questions.explanation: CSF exits the fourth ventricle through the foramina of Luschka (lateral) and Magendie (median) into the subarachnoid space surrounding the brainstem and cerebellum (cisterna magna).
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle CSF flows through Luschka and Magendie apertures into the subarachnoid space.
options: Subarachnoid space over the cerebral hemispheres

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which muscle is responsible for retraction of the mandible?
questions.explanation: The masseter muscle retracts the mandible (pulls it posteriorly). The temporalis also retracts, while the medial pterygoid and lateral pterygoid (lower head) protract the mandible.
questions.keyConcept: Masseter is the primary mandibular retractor; temporalis assists with retrusion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which response occurs in a stretch reflex?
questions.explanation: In a stretch reflex, muscle spindle afferents (Ia fibers) sense stretch and monosynaptically activate alpha motor neurons, causing contraction of the same muscle (homonymous muscle).
questions.keyConcept: Stretch reflex is a monosynaptic reflex where muscle spindle afferents directly excite homonymous alpha motor neurons.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which response occurs when the right foot is suddenly struck?
questions.explanation: A sudden foot strike (ankle jerk) causes dorsiflexion stretch of the gastrocnemius, activating muscle spindles that monosynaptically trigger calf muscle contraction (ankle jerk reflex).
questions.keyConcept: Ankle jerk is a stretch reflex where gastrocnemius stretch elicits contraction via Ia afferents to alpha motor neurons.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which receptor is primarily responsible for maintaining muscle tone?
questions.explanation: Primary endings of muscle spindles (Ia afferents) are primarily responsible for maintaining muscle tone through the stretch reflex arc controlling baseline contraction.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindle primary endings provide the major sensory input for tonic stretch reflex and tone maintenance.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which response occurs in a stretch reflex? (variant)
questions.explanation: In a stretch reflex, muscle spindle afferents detect stretch and monosynaptically activate alpha motor neurons causing homonymous muscle contraction, with gamma bias facilitating the response.
questions.keyConcept: Stretch reflex is monosynaptic: spindle afferents directly excite alpha motor neurons causing homonymous contraction.
options: Activation of gamma motor neurons only

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The supplementary motor area is primarily responsible for which function?
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (SMA) programs complex motor sequences and bimanual coordination, becoming active before voluntary movement initiation.
questions.keyConcept: SMA mediates motor sequence planning and bimanual coordination prior to primary motor cortex activation.
options: Control of complex movements of both hands

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Sudden, sustained dorsiflexion of the foot typically causes which response?
questions.explanation: Sudden dorsiflexion stretches the gastrocnemius, activating muscle spindles and triggering the stretch reflex (ankle jerk) causing plantarflexion.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsiflexion triggers gastrocnemius stretch reflex causing reflexive plantarflexion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which structure is primarily responsible for the damping action that prevents tremors during voluntary movements?
questions.explanation: The cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) is responsible for the damping action that prevents overshoot and tremors during voluntary movements through its feedback loops.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar damping mechanism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which amino acids are responsible for the characteristic burned sugar odor of urine in maple syrup urine disease?
questions.explanation: The branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine accumulate in maple syrup urine disease due to deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase.
questions.keyConcept: Maple syrup urine disease

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which mechanoreceptor is primarily responsible for detecting vibration?
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting deep pressure and vibration receptors with a characteristic onion-like lamellar structure located in dermis and deeper tissues.
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscle function

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Ascending sensory bundle in brain stem, end in diencephalon:
questions.explanation: The medial lemniscus is an ascending sensory bundle in the brainstem carrying fine touch and proprioception information, terminating in the VPL nucleus of thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Medial lemniscus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Concerning the fourth ventricle; choose the most correct answer:
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle roof is formed by the superior cerebellar peduncle (superior medullary velum) and inferior medullary velum, not the floor.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof
options: Its floor is formed by the closed medulla and pons.
Its roof is formed by the superior and inferior medullary vela.
Its choroids plexus is present in the floor of the ventricle.
It has a communication with the lateral ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg) the lesion is in one of the following arteries:
questions.explanation: Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome) results from PICA infarction, causing ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ataxia, and hoarseness.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral medullary syndrome

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 25‑year‑old woman presents with proximal, jerky, non‑purposeful movements of the limbs accompanied by hypotonia. Degeneration of which central nervous system structure is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Chorea (jerky, non-purposeful movements) with hypotonia results from caudate nucleus degeneration in Huntington disease, an autosomal dominant condition.
questions.keyConcept: Chorea pathophysiology
options: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which tract is responsible for spino‑visual reflexes (turning the head and eyes toward a cutaneous stimulus)?
questions.explanation: The spinotectal tract carries pain information to the superior colliculus for reflex head and eye movements toward cutaneous stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Spinotectal reflex

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which structure is present at the level of the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The central tegmental tract (carrying pallidal and cerebellar projections) is present at midbrain level, running between red nucleus and inferior olivary nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Midbrain structures

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is located in its:
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is located in the inferior roof (posterior medullary velum), not the floor or superior roof.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle choroid plexus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During the cotton wool test for crude touch, the receptors responsible are:
questions.explanation: Mechanoreceptors detect the light touch sensation tested by cotton wool; they include Meissner corpuscles and Merkel discs.
questions.keyConcept: Crude touch receptors

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with a lesion in the right cerebral peduncle (midbrain) would present with:
questions.explanation: Right cerebral peduncle lesion causes left-sided motor weakness (contralateral) because corticospinal fibers have already crossed at the pyramidal decussation.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral peduncle lesion
options: Loss of fine touch on the left side of the body
Loss of pain sensation on the right side
Skeletal motor loss on the entire left side

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which receptors are most likely responsible for the sudden muscle relaxation when a weight‑lifter releases a heavy load after a sustained hold?
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs (type Ib) detect muscle tension and trigger inverse stretch reflex causing sudden muscle relaxation when tension becomes dangerous.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi tendon reflex

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 3 external features of ventral pons:
questions.explanation: The ventral pons displays three characteristic features: the middle cerebellar peduncle laterally, the basilar artery groove centrally, and transverse grooves indicating underlying fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral pons features: middle cerebellar peduncle, basilar groove, transverse fibers.
questions.modelAnswer: MCP, Basilar artery sulcus, transverse grooves.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Borders of back of pons:
questions.explanation: The posterior surface of the pons is bounded by the medullary striae at its base (marking the pontomedullary junction), the cerebral aqueduct superiorly at the apex, and the floor consisting of the medial eminence, facial colliculus, and vestibular area.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior pons bounded by: medullary striae (base), cerebral aqueduct (apex), medial eminence/facial colliculus/vestibular area (floor).
questions.modelAnswer: Base: medullary striae; Apex: cerebral aqueduct; Floor: medial eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: External features of back of midbrain:
questions.explanation: The posterior midbrain displays four colliculi: two superior colliculi (involved in visual reflexes) and two inferior colliculi (involved in auditory reflexes), collectively forming the tectal plate or quadrigeminal plate.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior midbrain: two superior and two inferior colliculi.
questions.modelAnswer: 2 superior and 2 inferior colliculi.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Roof of fourth ventricle:
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle roof consists of two vela: the superior medullary velum (connecting the superior cerebellar peduncles) forms the upper roof, while the inferior medullary velum (with choroid plexus) forms the lower roof.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof: superior and inferior medullary vela.
questions.modelAnswer: Superiorly: SCP and superior medullary velum; Inferiorly: inferior medullary velum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Floor of fourth ventricle:
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle floor has two parts: the pontine part contains the medial eminence, facial colliculus, and vestibular area; the medullary part contains the hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, and vestibular trigone.
questions.keyConcept: Floor of fourth ventricle: pontine (medial eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area) and medullary (three trigones).
questions.modelAnswer: Pontine part (medial eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area); Medullary part (hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, vestibular trigone).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Arteries supplying pons:
questions.explanation: The pons is primarily supplied by paramedian and circumferential branches of the basilar artery, which penetrate the ventral surface to supply pontine nuclei and fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Pons supplied by branches of basilar artery.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of basilar artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Arteries supplying midbrain:
questions.explanation: The midbrain receives blood from branches of the posterior cerebral artery (supplying the anterior and lateral regions) and branches of the superior cerebellar artery (supplying the posterior region).
questions.keyConcept: Midbrain supplied by posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Medial medullary syndrome causes:
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (from occlusion of the anterior spinal artery or vertebral artery) causes contralateral spastic hemiplegia below the lesion, contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch, and ipsilateral flaccid tongue paralysis.
questions.keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome: contralateral hemiplegia, proprioception loss, ipsilateral tongue palsy.
questions.modelAnswer: Contralateral hemiplegia (flaccid), contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch, ipsilateral LMNL of tongue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lateral medullary syndrome causes:
questions.explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome from PICA occlusion) causes ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, hoarseness, and Horner syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral medullary syndrome: ipsilateral face, contralateral body sensory loss, ataxia, Horner syndrome.
questions.modelAnswer: Cerebellar ataxia, ipsilateral loss of pain/temp from face, contralateral loss from body, ipsilateral paralysis of palate/pharynx/larynx, loss of taste, ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve is responsible for the sensory innervation of the lower eyelid?
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (branch of V2) provides sensory innervation to the lower eyelid, upper lip, and cheek, entering through the infraorbital foramen on the anterior maxilla.
questions.keyConcept: Lower eyelid sensory innervation: infraorbital nerve (V2).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A tumor in the floor of the fourth ventricle (facial colliculus region) most directly damages which nucleus?
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus in the floor of the 4th ventricle overlies the abducent (CN VI) nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus: facial nerve wraps around abducens nucleus in floor of fourth ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The fourth ventricle communicates with the subarachnoid space through the median aperture, the:
questions.explanation: The median aperture (foramen of Magendie) drains CSF into the cisterna magna.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle communicates with subarachnoid space via lateral apertures of Luschka and median aperture of Magendie.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The primary motor cortex (area 4) is chiefly responsible for:
questions.explanation: Area 4 executes movement; planning is premotor/SMA.
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor cortex (area 4): execution of voluntary movement.
options: Sensory perception of limb position in space
Converting the plan into actual movement

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which ion is primarily responsible for rapid depolarization during an action potential?
questions.explanation: Sodium ions (Na+) rapid influx through voltage-gated channels cause the sharp upstroke of the action potential, taking the membrane potential from -70mV toward +30mV.
questions.keyConcept: Na+ influx causes rapid depolarization phase of action potential.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Muscle stretch reflex is facilitated by:
A. Medullary reticular formation
B. Cortical area 4
C. Red nucleus
D. Cortical area 6
E. Lentiform nucleus of basal ganglia
questions.explanation: The primary motor cortex (area 4) facilitates the muscle stretch reflex through corticospinal influences on gamma motor neurons that regulate muscle spindle sensitivity.
questions.keyConcept: Cortical area 4 facilitates stretch reflex via corticospinal influence on gamma neurons.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following nuclei affected in hemiballismus?
A. Caudate nucleus
B. Subthalamic nucleus
C. Substantia nigra
D. Lentiform
E. None of the above
questions.explanation: Hemiballismus is characterized by violent, flinging movements of contralateral limbs resulting from damage to the subthalamic nucleus, disrupting the indirect pathway of the basal ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: Hemiballismus: subthalamic nucleus lesion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The main input of the basal ganglia is to:
A. Caudate
B. Globus pallidus
C. Substantia Nigra
D. Subthalamic nucleus
E. None of the above
questions.explanation: The caudate nucleus (with putamen forming the striatum) is the main input structure of the basal ganglia, receiving excitatory corticostriatal projections and sending output via the globus pallidus.
questions.keyConcept: Main basal ganglia input: caudate nucleus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The phenomenon of decerebrate rigidity can be explained, at least in part, by which of the following?
A. Stimulation of type 1b sensory neurons
B. Loss of cerebellar inputs to the red nucleus
C. Overactivity of the medullary reticular nuclei involved in motor control
D. Unopposed activity of the pontine reticular nuclei
E. Degeneration of the nigrostriatal pathway
questions.explanation: Decerebrate rigidity results from loss of pontine reticular nucleus inhibition of medullary reticular nuclei, causing unopposed extensor muscle activity and characteristic rigid posturing.
questions.keyConcept: Decerebrate rigidity: unopposed medullary reticular nuclei activity from pontine loss.
options: Loss of cerebellar inputs to the red nucleus
Overactivity of the medullary reticular nuclei involved in motor control
Unopposed activity of the pontine reticular nuclei

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following events are present when we wake up in the morning?
A. Increased activity of anterior hypothalamus and RAS
B. Orexin is in its lowest levels
C. Light activates the pontine reticular formation
D. Norepinephrine and serotonin levels are usually high
E. Acetylcholine promotes wakefulness
questions.explanation: Upon waking, norepinephrine and serotonin levels are high, promoting wakefulness and alertness while orexin (hypocretin) levels rise to maintain arousal.
questions.keyConcept: Waking: high norepinephrine and serotonin, high orexin.
options: Increased activity of anterior hypothalamus and RAS
Orexin is in its lowest levels
Light activates the pontine reticular formation
Norepinephrine and serotonin levels are usually high

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The representational hemisphere is described by which one of the following?
A. It always lies in left hemisphere
B. It has no function
C. It is responsible for visuospatial relations
D. It is concerned with language
E. It contains speech Centre
questions.explanation: The representational (non-dominant) hemisphere, usually right, is responsible for visuospatial relationships and perceiving the spatial positions of objects in the environment.
questions.keyConcept: Representational hemisphere: visuospatial relations (usually right).
options: It always lies in left hemisphere
It is responsible for visuospatial relations

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The reward center is in which one of the following?
A. Lateral nucleus of hypothalamus
B. Broca's area
C. Cerebellum
D. Red nucleus
E. Arcuate fasciculus
questions.explanation: The reward (pleasure) center is located in the lateral hypothalamus; stimulation produces feelings of satisfaction and reinforces behaviors necessary for survival.
questions.keyConcept: Reward center: lateral hypothalamus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which area of hypothalamus is responsible for sexual behavior?
A. Supraoptic nucleus
B. Paraventricular nucleus
C. Anterior part of hypothalamus
D. Suprachiasmatic nucleus
E. Pre-optic nucleus
questions.explanation: The anterior hypothalamus contains structures essential for sexual behavior and mating, including the preoptic area which shows sex differences in neuron number.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior hypothalamus: sexual behavior.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following describes learning?
A. Memory is not essential for it
B. Sensitization means decreased response to repeated stimuli
C. Operant conditioning is a type of associative learning
D. Habituation and sensitization are types of conditioning learning
E. Habituation means increased response to repeated stimuli
questions.explanation: Operant (instrumental) conditioning is a type of associative learning where behavior is modified by consequences (reward or punishment), distinguishing it from non-associative learning.
questions.keyConcept: Operant conditioning: associative learning via consequences.
options: Memory is not essential for it
Sensitization means decreased response to repeated stimuli
Operant conditioning is a type of associative learning
Habituation and sensitization are types of conditioning learning
Habituation means increased response to repeated stimuli

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Corticonuclear fibers pass through ……… of internal capsule to reach the brain stem.
questions.explanation: Corticonuclear fibers (corticobulbar tract) pass through the genu (bend) of the internal capsule to reach brainstem cranial nerve nuclei for voluntary control of face and neck muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Corticonuclear fibers pass through genu of internal capsule.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Anterior cerebral artery is responsible for the supply of:
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the motor and sensory areas for the contralateral lower limb due to its course along the medial cerebral hemisphere.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery: supplies contralateral lower limb motor/sensory areas.
options: Sensory and motor areas of the contralateral upper limb.
Sensory and motor areas of the contralateral lower limb.
